extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing Section 101 (judicial-exception) eligibility analyses, focusing on whether claim additional elements meaningfully limit a judicial exception (e.g., are they more than 'apply it', are they insignificant extra‑solution activity, or merely a field-of-use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere Instructions To Apply An Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the additional elements amount to more than a recitation of the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent) or are more than mere instructions to implement an abstract idea or other judicial exception on a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The additional element(s) must do more than simply state the judicial exception while adding the words 'apply it' (Alice; Mayo). Claims that are nothing more than an instruction to apply an abstract idea using a generic computer do not render the idea eligible. Examiners should, when appropriate, explain on the record why additional elements do not meaningfully limit the judicial exception and may rely on overlap with other considerations (improvement, particular machine, particular transformation, well‑understood/routine/conventional — noting well‑understood/routine/conventional is evaluated in Step 2B only). Examiners should see MPEP §2106.07(a) for formulating subject matter eligibility rejections. Examples & case guidance: Mayo (measuring metabolites was merely instructive), Alice (generic computer recitation amounted to 'apply it'), Benson (conversion algorithm had no meaningful practical application except on a computer). Cases finding technological solutions that are more than 'apply it' include DDR Holdings (manipulating Internet interactions to produce a desired result), BASCOM (ISP‑located filtering tool with user‑specific customizable filtering), McRO, Thales Visionix (particular sensor configuration and data use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity vs. Result-Oriented Recitation (consideration under 'apply it')
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim merely recites the idea of a solution or outcome (result-oriented, functionally stated) without details of how the solution is accomplished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that attempt to cover any solution to an identified problem with no restriction on how the result is accomplished and no description of the mechanism do not integrate a judicial exception into a practical application (equivalent to 'apply it'). By contrast, claiming a particular solution or a particular way to achieve a desired outcome may integrate the exception into a practical application. Cases: Electric Power Group (caution against claims so result-focused as to cover any solution), Intellectual Ventures/Capital One (XML example: merely using abstract idea in context of XML without specifying how), Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network (maintaining state of data without mechanism described).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invoking Computers or Machinery Merely as a Tool (consideration under 'apply it')
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim invokes a computer or other machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process (i.e., using machines in their ordinary capacity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a general-purpose computer or adding generic computer components to an abstract idea does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more (Alice, Gottschalk v. Benson, Versata, TLI, Affinity Labs). Claiming improved speed or efficiency solely because of a general-purpose computer is insufficient. In contrast, claims that improve computer capabilities or an existing technology may provide significantly more (McRO, Enfish). Examples of tool-only invocations: telephone unit and server used in ordinary capacity to record, administer, archive images (TLI); applying commonplace business method or algorithm on a general-purpose computer (Alice/Benson); generating menus with generic computer components (Ameranth); monitoring audit logs on a general-purpose computer where speed improvements derive solely from the computer (FairWarning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity/Generality of the Application of the Judicial Exception (consideration under 'apply it')
rubrics_metrics.description: How particular or general is the claimed application of the judicial exception across fields of endeavor and modes of accomplishing the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim with broad applicability across many fields that generically recites an effect or claims every mode of accomplishing that effect may amount to merely adding 'apply it' and not provide meaningful limitations (O’Reilly v. Morse, The Telephone Cases, Internet Patents Corp.). Limitations that confine the exception to a particular, practical application may amount to significantly more (BASCOM: specific ISP‑located filtering tool with per‑user customization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant Extra‑Solution Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether additional elements add more than insignificant extra‑solution activity to the judicial exception; 'extra‑solution activity' are activities incidental to the primary process/product (pre‑solution or post‑solution) that are nominal or tangential additions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insignificant extra‑solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, routine post‑solution output) does not amount to an inventive concept, particularly when well‑understood or conventional (Parker v. Flook; Mayo). Examiners should consider overlap with particular machine/particular transformation and field-of-use/technological environment considerations; however, well‑understood/routine/conventional is evaluated in Step 2B and should not be considered in Step 2A Prong Two. Examiners should explain in rejections why such elements do not meaningfully limit the claim (see MPEP §2106.07(a)). Examples of extra-solution activity: pre‑solution data gathering (e.g., obtaining credit card transaction info), post‑solution output (e.g., printing a report), testing to obtain inputs, presenting offers and gathering response statistics. Cases: Flook (post‑solution alarm limit adjustment), Mayo (measuring metabolites), OIP Technologies (presenting offers and gathering statistics), CyberSource (verifying transactions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for Determining Insignificant Extra‑Solution Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations to decide if an additional element is insignificant extra‑solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may consider: (1) Whether the extra‑solution limitation is well known — token or conventional activities (cases: Bilski, Flook, Intellectual Ventures/Erie). Note overlap with well‑understood/routine/conventional (not to be used in Step 2A Prong Two). (2) Whether the limitation is significant — does it impose meaningful limits on the claim so it is not nominally/tangentially related (cases: Ultramercial v. Hulu, Apple v. Ameranth). This factor is considered in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. (3) Whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting — i.e., all uses of the recited judicial exception require such data gathering or output (cases: Mayo; OIP Technologies). This is considered in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of Insignificant Extra‑Solution Activity (illustrative categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete examples and categories of activities courts have found to be insignificant extra‑solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere data gathering examples: clinical tests to obtain equation inputs (In re Grams), system testing to determine response (In re Meyers), presenting offers and gathering response statistics (OIP Technologies), obtaining transaction info to verify credit card transactions (CyberSource), consulting/updating logs (Ultramercial), determining biomarker levels in blood (Mayo). Selecting particular data sources/types: limiting index to XML tags (Intellectual Ventures/Erie), taking orders from only certain customer types (Ameranth), selecting power‑grid info for analysis (Electric Power Group), requiring user request to view advertisement (Ultramercial). Insignificant application examples: cutting hair after determining style (In re Brown), printing/downloading generated menus (Ameranth). Some cases identify insignificant computer implementation as an example (Fort Properties; Bancorp Services), while others treat such limitations as mere instructions to apply the exception (see MPEP §2106.05(f)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of Use and Technological Environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether additional elements do more than generally link the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use or adding token post‑solution components does not make the concept patentable (Parker v. Flook; Bilski). A claim cannot be made eligible simply by acquiescing to limiting the formula's reach to a particular technological use (Diamond v. Diehr). Examiners should treat mere field‑of‑use/technological environment limitations as not providing significantly more than the judicial exception. Example: Flook — mathematical formula applied in a catalytic chemical process was insufficient to render patentable.
